poiCNS-desc:
Conosur is the bloc of the Southern Cone: Argentina and Chile, bound together at the bottom of the world. Its wealth is copper above all, with some lithium in the north, and it has little oil or gas of its own. Through Patagonia it is the gateway to the far south, and it shares a quiet, profitable link with the Antarctica Trust.

Argentina is the larger partner and the louder one. When the walls of Buenos Aires fell in 2132, anarchy swept its provinces, and it has spent the decades since trying to put itself back together under a Grand Council of factions that cannot stand one another. Chile, sheltered behind the Andes and facing the Pacific, is the steadier half of the bloc.

To the north lies the Andean Compact, rich, confident and never far from the Cone's affairs. Refugees from Argentina's wars still spill across the Compact's southern outposts, and Lima has long debated whether to back one Argentine faction or supply all of them and keep the south divided and weak. Conosur's future depends on whether Argentina can rule itself before someone else decides to do it for it.
poiCNS001-desc:
When the great walls of Buenos Aires fell in 2132, Argentina changed forever. Anarchy swept the provinces, and many forgot the very idea of Argentina. A new capital, Nuevos Aires, rose in the old one's place, and around it the country has been slowly, violently reassembled.

The government's writ runs in the cities. In the villages and remote settlements, nobody is sure it runs at all. Rather than project power it does not have, the capital signs deals with local industrial and agricultural centres, sends them aid to keep them afloat, and makes sure they never grow strong enough to band together against it. Not too little power, and not too much.
poiCNS002-desc:
Argentina is not run by one person. It is led by the Grand Council, where four factions that cannot stand one another are forced to coexist.

The Urbanites, capitalists, entrepreneurs and intellectuals, have made Nuevos Aires a beacon for the rich. Their donations pad the national budget, their investments fill the research institutes, and they have become the foundation of the coalition. The Argentinists, radical officers who still believe the idea of Argentina is worth any conquest, have been made the regime's spear, and grow stronger every day. The Federales, rising from the civil governments, bureaucrats and police who held the provinces together after Buenos Aires fell, resent the focus on the capital and resist both unification and urbanization. The Montoneros, a leftist guerrilla movement drawn from the hungry countryside, preach agrarian socialism and openly defy the military's orders.

The future of Argentina will be decided by the machinations in the Council's halls.
